speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: asked the Minister for Finance (a) whether he can provide a detailed account of the recent spate of Wage Credit Scheme claims; (b) what are the countermeasures taken; and (c) whether a full review will be undertaken to prevent future breaches.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Minister for Finance in light of recent fraudulent claims made under the Productivity and Innovation Credit, Wage Credit Scheme and SkillsFuture (a) what considerations determine whether additional audits or investigations of a forensic nature ought to be carried out for claims under these schemes; and (b) whether there is any threshold of fraudulent claims which can lead to the suspension/review of such Government schemes in view of the administrative burden of assessing fraudulent claims.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For businesses, especially small and medium enterprises, the PIC provides funding support so that they can become more productive and, hence, more profitable over time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Through WCS, the Government supports businesses by sharing in sustainable wage growth for workers, especially for our lower- and middle-income workers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As for SkillsFuture, this is a national movement to empower individuals to take charge of their own learning and adapt to a changing world.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This includes the recent payout in 2017, where more than $0.6 billion of Wage Credit payouts were made to over 85,000 employers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The vast majority of these payouts were denied upfront, with the remainder being clawed back by IRAS largely within a year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These figures cover cases of attempted fraud which IRAS detected and acted against over the four-year period.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The media had reported the figures recently, but they were not a recent phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the 1,000 cases were all acted upon over the entire period of WCS, since it started.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But IRAS recently publicised these figures to caution employers against attempts to abuse or game the system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Pritam Singh also asked how Government agencies go about investigating fraudulent claims.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Minister for Higher Education and Skills has covered SkillsFuture, and so I will cover WCS and PIC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Essentially, IRAS uses a risk-based approach to safeguard against abuse.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This methodology is used for all IRAS programmes, including WCS and PIC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All potential WCS payouts and PIC applications are first checked upfront against a set of predetermined criteria for signs that indicate possible gaming.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is complemented by the use of analytics, field intelligence and other sources of information, including a whistleblowing platform.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Cases that are assessed to be of a higher-risk profile, say, claim amounts that are not commensurate with the scale of the business, are subject to more detailed investigations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For WCS, this may entail examination of supporting documents, such as payslips and bank statements, and conducting phone interviews to verify the authenticity and accuracy of the submitted wage increases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For PIC, this may entail examination of transaction details and verification of documents, such as suppliers' invoices and payment evidence.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS may also conduct field visits to understand the applicant’s business, for example, how the PIC equipment is used in the business.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS will continue to take strict enforcement and legal actions against those who abuse the schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This includes disqualifying offenders from other Government schemes and taking legal action against such offenders.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Offenders can be charged under the Penal Code or the Income Tax Act for abusing the schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More generally, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) undertakes periodic reviews of Government schemes to ensure that they are relevant and achieve the purposes that they are designed for.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Programmes which continue to serve their purpose will be retained.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Others, which are intended to be time-limited, will be terminated at their end-date.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yet others may be continued with revised criteria, based on the actual experience of running the schemes and the assessment of the scheme’s overall effectiveness, which includes a weighing of the scheme’s benefits against its administrative costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I refer to the latest Estimates Committee Report where it was made known that about 313,000 PIC cash payouts have been submitted over the years and 98,000 ­– almost one third of them – were selected for review and, out of that number, 64% of the claims were rejected upfront.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reply from MOF to the Estimates Committee also stated that for the remaining 215,000 PIC claims, I quote, "they may be selected for review based on other factors".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Are there any additional factors that IRAS specifically considers for claims which fall outside their usual risk-based approach?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From the reading of MOF's reply to the Estimates Committee, it appears that more review is going to be done for claims which were not originally audited.
